headline.headline: REDS SURVIVE PITTSBURGH RALLY, STEAL SERIES WIN WITH THREE IN THE NINTH
headline.deck: Cincinnati storms back in final frame to outlast Pirates, 9-7, at PNC Park
headline.body:
PITTSBURGH -- The Cincinnati Reds refused to let PNC Park swallow them whole Saturday night, scoring three runs in the top of the ninth inning to survive a tenacious Pittsburgh Pirates rally and escape with a 9-7 victory before 30,077 fans.

The Pirates had clawed back from a 6-4 deficit with two runs in the seventh and one more in the eighth to make it a one-run game heading into the final frame, but Cincinnati's offense had one more answer. The Reds had taken an early lead with single runs in the first and third innings, Pittsburgh briefly seized control with three in the third, and the back-and-forth brawl stretched across three hours and six minutes, including a 36-minute delay. Pitcher Jones earned the win for Cincinnati, picking up his second decision of the night in relief, while Christian Arroyo was hit by a pitch from Ramírez in a game that never lacked for friction.

The victory moves Cincinnati above the .500 mark at a critical stretch of the season and hands Pittsburgh another gut-punch defeat in a home series they desperately needed. For the Reds, three runs in the ninth -- when the Pirates bullpen had nothing left -- was the difference between a road win and a devastating late collapse.

secondary.headline: RED SOX SILENCE YANKEES, 4-1, AS RIVALRY SWINGS HARD TOWARD BOSTON
secondary.deck: Schuemann homers as Boston holds New York scoreless for eight innings at Fenway
secondary.body:
BOSTON -- The Boston Red Sox handed the New York Yankees a thorough beating Saturday afternoon at Fenway Park, winning 4-1 before 36,026 fans in a game that was never really in doubt after the third inning. Boston scored in each of the first three innings, building a 4-0 cushion before New York finally dented the scoreboard with a lone run in the fifth. Schuemann provided the signature blow, launching a home run -- his first of the season -- to help pace the Boston attack.

The Yankees were held to a single run across nine innings, with their lineup unable to generate any sustained pressure against Boston's pitching staff. The loss tightens New York's grip on the AL East standings at a time when they can least afford it, while Boston continues to build momentum heading into the final days of June. The game took 2 hours and 22 minutes, a mercifully efficient outcome for a crowd that witnessed their team dominate the rivalry game from wire to wire.

secondary.headline: SHARKS DRAFT HISTORY WITH 7-FOOT-1 KARMANOV, UPENDING EVERYTHING SCOUTS KNOW
secondary.deck: San Jose selects tallest player ever drafted in NHL, reshaping how teams think about size on blue line
secondary.body:
San Jose made the most audacious pick of the 2026 NHL Draft on Saturday, selecting 18-year-old defenseman Alexander Karmanov with a selection that immediately rewrote the record books. At 7 feet 1 inch tall, Karmanov is the largest player ever drafted in the history of the NHL, and his arrival in San Jose's prospect pipeline sets the hockey world buzzing about what a player of that frame can do on the blue line at the professional level.

The Sharks, rebuilding after several difficult seasons, are swinging for the fences with a pick that scouts and analysts are still scrambling to evaluate. No player of Karmanov's height has ever reached the NHL, making this either the most visionary selection of the draft weekend or its most spectacular gamble. Draft grades across the league ranged from cautious praise to outright skepticism, but nobody in the building Saturday was talking about any other pick. San Jose has made its statement.

secondary.headline: METS BLUDGEON PHILLIES, 6-2, AS LINDOR, SOTO POWER LATE SURGE AT CITI FIELD
secondary.deck: New York erupts for four runs in sixth and two more in seventh to flip script on Philadelphia
secondary.body:
NEW YORK -- The New York Mets trailed the Philadelphia Phillies 2-0 through five innings Saturday evening at Citi Field, looking like a team that might sleepwalk through the home stand. Then the sixth inning arrived, and Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto did not. The Mets scored four times in the sixth and added two more in the seventh to walk away with a commanding 6-2 victory before 37,338 fans, handing Bryce Harper and the Phillies their most lopsided loss of the series. Harper had slugged his 19th home run of the season in the third inning to put Philadelphia ahead, and for a time it looked like enough.

But Lindor tripled, Soto tripled, and the Mets' middle of the lineup simply overwhelmed a Phillies bullpen that could not hold a two-run lead into the sixth. The game was delayed 1 hour and 10 minutes at some point, but the Mets emerged from the stoppage sharper than they went in. For Philadelphia, the loss stings: Harper provided the firepower, and the bullpen gave it all back. The NL East race tightens as June ends.

column.headline: THE NINTH INNING IS WHERE BASEBALL TELLS THE TRUTH
column.body:
Saturday night in Pittsburgh, the Cincinnati Reds reminded every casual fan why you never leave a baseball game early and never close the app before the final out. Three runs in the ninth inning, against a Pirates team that had fought back from a five-run hole to make it a one-run game -- that is not strategy, that is nerve. Pittsburgh had momentum, Pittsburgh had the crowd, Pittsburgh had everything except the final three outs. The Reds took those too.

And over in Boston, the Yankees walked into Fenway and got systematically dismantled by a Red Sox team that spotted them a run and still won by three. The AL East race is tightening in every direction at once. Tampa Bay leads the division, Boston is surging, and New York is running out of June. The last week of the first half of the season has a way of separating the contenders from the pretenders, and right now the pretenders are wearing pinstripes.

story.headline: ASTROS RALLY PAST TIGERS IN SLUGFEST, 8-6, AS HOUSTON ERUPTS FOR THREE IN EIGHTH
story.deck: Houston overcomes Detroit's early advantage with a big eighth inning at Comerica Park.
story.body:
DETROIT, June 27 -- The Houston Astros spotted Detroit a four-run third inning, fell behind by multiple runs, and still walked out of Comerica Park with an 8-6 victory Saturday night, capping their comeback with a three-run eighth inning before 27,232 fans. Smith launched his ninth homer of the season, Carpenter connected for his 12th, and Lee added his third as Houston battered Tigers pitching for eight runs on a humid summer evening that lasted 2 hours and 46 minutes.

Detroit staked itself to a 4-3 lead after three innings, getting its biggest burst in the third frame when the Tigers plated four runs against the Astros staff. Houston chipped away with single runs in the fourth and seventh to keep pace, but the game turned decisively in the eighth when the Astros pushed across three runs to seize a lead they would not relinquish. Spencer Torkelson, hit by a pitch from Teng during the contest, was among the Tigers who doubled, with Paredes, Walker, Greene, and McKinstry also collecting two-base hits for Detroit.

Despite leaving 24 runners on base, the Tigers could not deliver the clutch hits necessary to hold off Houston's relentless lineup, which stranded 18 of its own. The Astros' offensive depth proved the difference, with the middle of their order doing the most damage in the eighth and the long ball carrying Houston whenever the offense stalled in the earlier frames.

story.headline: MAGIC WAIVE ISAAC, CLEARING $6.5M AS NBA'S SPENDING FRENZY BEGINS
story.deck: Orlando cuts ties with the injury-plagued forward as front offices scramble for cap space.
story.body:
The Orlando Magic made a decisive financial move Saturday, waiving forward Jonathan Isaac and shedding $6.5 million from their books just as the NBA's free agency period loomed on the horizon. The decision, confirmed by ESPN's Bobby Marks, closes a painful chapter for both the 28-year-old Isaac and a franchise that watched his once-promising career dissolve into a cascade of serious injuries, including a torn ACL that cost him nearly two full seasons.

Isaac, the sixth overall pick in the 2017 draft, never fully recaptured the defensive brilliance that made him one of the most coveted young forwards in the Eastern Conference. Across nine seasons in Orlando, he played in fewer than 200 games, a heartbreaking return on a four-year, $80 million maximum extension the Magic signed in 2020. The waiving clears crucial flexibility for a young Orlando core that includes Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner as the franchise attempts to build genuine title contention.

Elsewhere around the league, Jimmy Butler offered cautious optimism Saturday regarding his recovery from the right ACL tear he suffered January 19 with Golden State, telling ESPN he expects to return as "a top player." The Warriors, already navigating a complicated salary sheet, will monitor Butler's rehab closely as roster decisions mount. Meanwhile, Bobby Marks' league-wide spending power breakdown illustrated starkly which franchises enter this summer with room to maneuver and which front offices are white-knuckling their way beneath the punishing second apron threshold.

story.headline: SHARKS MAKE HISTORY WITH TOWERING PICK AS 2026 NHL DRAFT DELIVERS STUNNING MOMENTS
story.deck: San Jose selects 7-foot-1 Alexander Karmanov, the tallest player ever drafted in league history.
story.body:
The 2026 NHL Draft will be remembered for many things, but none more striking than the San Jose Sharks stepping to the podium and selecting Alexander Karmanov, an 18-year-old Russian defenseman who stands 7-foot-1 and instantly became the tallest player ever drafted in the history of the league. The mammoth blueliner, whose wingspan and reach present matchup nightmares that NHL scouts have never quite encountered before, gives a rebuilding Sharks franchise a potential cornerstone piece unlike anything the sport has seen. Whether that size translates to NHL dominance remains the ultimate question, but San Jose's front office clearly believes the upside justifies the gamble.

Beyond the Karmanov spectacle, analysts wasted no time rendering verdicts on which franchises helped themselves most over the weekend and which left the draft floor with questions to answer. The New York Rangers, Toronto Maple Leafs and Chicago Blackhawks emerged as widely cited winners, drawing praise for targeting high-ceiling forwards and defensemen projected to accelerate their respective timelines. Several other clubs, however, drew sharp criticism for reaches that puzzled draft boards and raised eyebrows among scouts who had dramatically different players ranked in those slots.

With seven rounds complete and all 32 teams having made their selections, the work now shifts from the draft floor to development camps and training facilities. Fantasy hockey managers are already mining the results, with several top picks drawing early enthusiasm as potential contributors as soon as next season. The draft's full impact will take years to measure, but one image will endure regardless: Alexander Karmanov ducking through a doorway somewhere in San Jose, daring the hockey world to imagine what comes next.

story.headline: QUARTERBACK CAROUSEL SPINS WILDLY AS NFL TEAMS RESHAPE ROSTERS FOR 2026
story.deck: Veteran signal-callers change addresses while draft picks brace for starting roles.
story.body:
The NFL offseason has turned into a full-blown quarterback frenzy, with franchises scrambling to secure signal-callers ahead of the 2026 season. The Cleveland Browns, still searching for stability under center, reached an agreement with veteran Kirk Cousins on a restructured deal after his release from the Atlanta Falcons, while the Las Vegas Raiders moved aggressively to acquire a proven starter through trade rather than trust an unproven roster heading into a critical year for the organization under new ownership.

The 2026 NFL Draft in Detroit delivered several quarterbacks to needy franchises, with analysts widely praising the selections made by the New Orleans Saints and the New York Giants, both of whom grabbed highly touted prospects in the first round. Saints general manager Mickey Loomis called the team's pick a cornerstone move for the next decade, a sentiment echoed across the league as rebuilding clubs bet heavily on young arms to replace aging or departed veterans.

Training camp storylines are already taking shape well ahead of the July reporting dates. The Dallas Cowboys, navigating life after a significant salary cap overhaul, are watching veteran wide receiver CeeDee Lamb's contract situation closely, with negotiations described by sources as cordial but unresolved. Meanwhile, the defending Super Bowl LX champion Kansas City Chiefs continue adding depth pieces through free agency, determined to sustain the dynasty Patrick Mahomes has anchored through what is now a remarkable run of championship contention.
